introduction_markdown: Time allowed: two and a half hours. Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1 1/2 hours; you are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II, answer all questions choosing EITHER parts a, b and c OR parts d, e and f of each question. For your guidance, the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration of free fall, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define specific latent heat of vaporization. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Why is the specific latent heat of vaporization of water much larger than its specific heat capacity? *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The specific latent heat of vaporization of a substance is the **quantity of heat required to change a unit mass (1 kg) of the liquid into vapour at its boiling point, without any change of temperature**. Unit: $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

(ii) The specific heat capacity only measures the energy needed to **raise the temperature** by one degree, which just increases the kinetic energy of the molecules, which stay together in the liquid. The latent heat of vaporization is the energy needed to **completely separate the molecules** against the strong forces of attraction between them, **and** to push back the atmosphere as the liquid expands into a vapour of much larger volume. This takes far more energy, so the latent heat is much larger.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The mercury column of a newly made mercury-in-glass thermometer is $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ long when the bulb is dipped in pure melting ice. When the bulb is transferred into steam from pure boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure, the mercury column is $17\,\mathrm{cm}$ long. When the bulb is dipped into another liquid of unknown temperature, $\theta$, the mercury column is $10\,\mathrm{cm}$ long.

(i) What is the thermometric property of this thermometer? *[1 mark]*

(ii) Calculate the unknown temperature, $\theta$, in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The thermometric property is the **length of the mercury column**.

(ii) Lower fixed point ($0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$): $5\,\mathrm{cm}$. Upper fixed point ($100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$): $17\,\mathrm{cm}$.

$\theta = \dfrac{l_\theta - l_0}{l_{100} - l_0}\times 100 = \dfrac{10 - 5}{17 - 5}\times 100 = \dfrac{5}{12}\times 100 = 41.7\,^\circ\mathrm{C} \approx 42\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$
